sections.title: Why the traditional concept of meaning needs revision

source_span.start_text: Language is the first broad area
source_span.end_text: a concept which rests on a false theory.

sections.summary: Putnam contrasts progress in syntax with the confused treatment of word meaning, then examines extension, intension, and their idealizations. Two traditional assumptions—that knowing meaning is an individual psychological state and that meaning determines extension—are identified as jointly untenable.

sections.title: Psychological states and methodological solipsism

source_span.start_text: In order to show this, we need first
source_span.end_text: We shall consider these alternatives later.

sections.summary: Narrow psychological states exclude dependence on other people or external objects, unlike ordinary relational mental states. Combining this restriction with traditional semantics implies that identical psychological states fix identical extensions, the consequence the essay will challenge.

sections.title: Twin Earth and externally determined reference

source_span.start_text: That psychological state does not determine extension

sections.summary: Twin Earth cases involving water and metals show that psychologically identical speakers can refer to different substances. Ordinary ignorance about elms and beeches extends the argument to familiar language, separating reference from an individual’s descriptive concepts.

sections.title: The division of linguistic labor

source_span.start_text: The last two examples depend upon a fact about language
source_span.end_text: Words have been thought of too much on the model of the first sort of tool.

sections.summary: Speakers depend on experts and coordinated social practices to fix the application of many terms. Putnam proposes a sociolinguistic universality hypothesis and distinguishes community competence from what any one speaker knows.

sections.title: Ostension and rigid reference across possible worlds

source_span.start_text: The first of our science-fiction examples

sections.summary: Natural-kind words are introduced through exemplars and stereotypes without making their identifying descriptions synonymous with the terms. Ostensive reference fixes a relation to actual samples, supporting a rigid rather than world-relative interpretation.

sections.title: Necessity, discovery, and indexical meaning

source_span.start_text: What Kripke was the first to observe
source_span.end_text: I mean that properties in this sense are not used at all.

sections.summary: Discovering a substance’s nature can establish a metaphysically necessary identity that was not knowable a priori. The indexical link to local exemplars explains how natural-kind terms can retain reference while speakers’ recognition methods and knowledge change.

sections.title: Realism against operational definitions

source_span.start_text: I wish now to contrast my view
source_span.end_text: things satisfying the description normally possess.

sections.summary: The gold example challenges the claim that a term’s extension is whatever passes contemporary tests. Scientific fallibility and changing theories remain compatible with stable reference, whereas operationalist and antirealist alternatives must address their consequences for truth and cross-theory communication.

sections.title: Context, alternative senses, and hidden structures

source_span.start_text: What we have analyzed so far
source_span.end_text: superficial characteristics become the decisive ones.

sections.summary: Context and interests influence which similarities matter, allowing ordinary, technical, and extended uses of natural-kind words. Hidden structure need not be unique or even present, as examples involving lemons, diseases, and jade qualify the core account.

sections.title: Artifacts and the reach of the externalist account

source_span.start_text: So far we have only used natural-kind words
source_span.end_text: took part in the action signified by the verb.

sections.summary: Pencil-organism and robot-cat cases extend rigid, indexical reference beyond familiar natural kinds and distinguish discovery from synonymy or conceptual impossibility. Artifact names and many other parts of speech can behave similarly, while some derivative and grammatical words retain a more purely criterial character.

sections.title: Separating extension from individual competence

source_span.start_text: Let us now see where we are
source_span.end_text: To this topic we now turn.

sections.summary: Meaning can be reconstructed as a structured vector including extension rather than identified with an individual concept. This separates sociolinguistic questions about reference from psycholinguistic questions about the ideas and skills required for competent use.

sections.title: Minimum competence for communication

source_span.end_text: not the abstract difficulty that Quine is talking about.

sections.summary: Correctly assigned extension alone does not amount to acquiring a word; speakers must meet culturally variable minimum standards of knowledge and use. Tiger and tree examples show how stereotypes support communication without requiring universal expert discrimination.

sections.title: Stereotypes without analytic guarantees

source_span.start_text: the notion of a ‘stereotype’ in my lectures
source_span.end_text: pretty accurate as far as they go.

sections.summary: Stereotypes are socially required conventional conceptions that can be incomplete or mistaken. Their usefulness for communication does not make associated features necessary, universal, or analytically true of a kind.

sections.title: Testing linguistic obligations

source_span.end_text: we shall not pursue this possibility here.

sections.summary: Idealized teaching and elicitation experiments illustrate how obligatory stereotype features could be investigated. Such behavioral consequences provide evidence without reducing theoretical notions to operational definitions or denying speakers’ own linguistic knowledge.

sections.title: Meaning after the critique of analyticity

source_span.end_text: no circularity of the kind Quine criticized appears here.

sections.summary: Putnam reviews Quine’s criticisms of analyticity, centrality, synonymy, and unrevisability, including the pressure from scientific theory change. Obligatory stereotype knowledge can remain part of meaning without guaranteeing truth or analyticity, avoiding those particular objections.

sections.title: Constraints on radical translation

source_span.start_text: What our theory does not do
source_span.end_text: Discussion of these matters will be deferred to another paper.

sections.summary: Stereotypes, expert-guided extensions, and elicited explanations constrain translation without independently determining it. Putnam argues for a wider evidence base than assent and dissent, while acknowledging the need for cultural and belief-related constraints.

sections.title: Why truth conditions do not exhaust meaning

source_span.start_text: In a series of publications, Donald Davidson
source_span.end_text: every success ever attained in the study of natural language has been based.

sections.summary: Davidsonian truth-theoretic semantics faces a tension between extensional correctness, informative translation, and avoiding the word being explained. Putnam also rejects restricting linguistic evidence to whole-sentence dispositions when constituent-level elicitation and native competence are available.

sections.title: Limits of possible-world intensions

source_span.start_text: I wish now to consider an approach
source_span.end_text: the philosophy of language underlying the earlier versions of the view.

sections.summary: Carnap-style intensions leave their psychological grasp unexplained and omit social cooperation and indexical reference. Vagueness does not repair these defects, though enriched formal models that include speakers and contexts may remain useful.

sections.title: Semantic markers as central classifications

source_span.start_text: If the approach suggested here is correct
source_span.end_text: an important contribution, when taken as suggested here.

sections.summary: Semantic markers identify highly central category features such as animal or artifact without making them absolutely unrevisable. Putnam preserves the distinction between markers and other stereotype features while rejecting their use as necessary-and-sufficient definitions.

sections.title: A normal form for meaning and its consequences

source_span.start_text: We may now summarize what has been said
source_span.end_text: a better philosophy and a better science of language must encompass both.

sections.summary: The proposed meaning vector includes syntactic markers, semantic markers, stereotype, and extension, with the last component not attributed to individual knowledge. Twin Earth and bilingual synonymy illustrate its consequences, and the conclusion calls for semantics that includes society and the external world.
